question: Buying a house this winter -- what can snow and cold hide from a home inspection?
verdictConfirmed: A winter inspection is still worth doing, but a state standard of practice (Washington's WAC 308-408C, read in full) lets inspectors leave snow and ice in place, skip a roof walk, skip winterized systems and not run air conditioning below 60 F. The report has to say how the roof was inspected. The usual 'escrow it till spring' advice comes from Fannie Mae's rules for new or proposed construction; on an existing house, items affecting safety or soundness (its examples include worn roof shingles) must be completed and verified before the loan is sold.

facts.claim: WAC 308-408C-010: a home inspection is not technically exhaustive and does not identify concealed conditions or latent defects; the SOP applies to buildings with four or fewer units
facts.quote: A home inspection is not technically exhaustive and does not identify concealed conditions or latent defects. This SOP is applicable to buildings with four or fewer dwelling units and their attached garages or carports.
facts.method: browser + curl of the full chapter

facts.claim: Chapter refiled WSR 26-15-037, filed 7/7/26, effective 8/7/26 (the current text)
WAC 308-408C-030(16): inspectors are not required to move snow, ice, soil, plants, furniture or debris
facts.quote: Inspectors are not required to: ... (16) Move suspended ceiling tiles, personal property, furniture, equipment, plants, soil, snow, ice or debris.

facts.claim: WAC 308-408C-090 roof: includes covering, gutters and downspouts, flashings, vents, skylights, penetrations, visible chimney; inspector traverses or uses alternate methods; inspects gutters and downspouts; not required to traverse where unsafe or damaging but must report the alternate method; not required to remove snow or ice; not required to predict remaining life
facts.quote: An inspection of the roof includes the roof covering materials; gutters and downspout systems; visible flashings; roof vents; skylights, and any other roof penetrations; and the portions of the chimneys and flues visible from the exterior. (1) The inspector will: • Traverse the roof to inspect it, or at the discretion of the home inspector, use alternate methods to inspect and report on condition. • Inspect the gutters and downspout systems, visible flashings, soffits and fascias, skylights, and other roof penetrations. ... (2) The inspector is not required to: • Traverse a roof where, in the opinion of the inspector, doing so can damage roofing materials or be unsafe. If the roof is not traversed, the alternate method used to inspect the roof must be reported. • Remove snow, ice, debris or other material that obscures the roof surface or prevents access to the roof. ... • Predict remaining life expectancy of roof coverings.

facts.claim: WAC 308-408C-080 exterior: inspects visible wall coverings, attached decks, steps, porches; probes where deterioration suspected; not required to inspect detached decks, patios, retaining walls, or enter under decks with less than five feet of clearance
facts.quote: An inspection of the exterior includes the visible wall coverings, trim, protective coatings and sealants, windows and doors, attached porches, decks, steps, balconies, handrails, guardrails, carports, eaves, soffits, fascias and visible exterior portions of chimneys. ... Probe exterior components where deterioration is suspected or where clear indications of possible deterioration exist. ... (2) The inspector is not required to: • Inspect (a) Buildings, decks, patios, fences, retaining walls, and other structures detached from the dwelling. ... • Enter areas beneath decks with less than five feet of clearance from the underside of joists to grade.

facts.claim: WAC 308-408C-070 structure: inspects visible, exposed foundations
facts.quote: The condition of visible, exposed foundations and grade slabs, walls, posts, piers, beams, joists, trusses, subfloors, chimney foundations, stairs and the visible roof structure and attic components.

facts.claim: WAC 308-408C-100(2)(b)(i) plumbing: not required to inspect any system that is shut down or winterized; also floor drains and exterior drains such as driveway drains
facts.quote: (2) The inspector is not required to: ... (b) Inspect (i) Any system that is shut down or winterized. (ii) Any plumbing components not readily accessible. (iii) Floor drains and exterior drain systems including, but not limited to, exterior stairwell drains and driveway drains.

facts.claim: WAC 308-408C-130 air conditioning/heat pumps: operate the system using normal controls; heat pumps can be tested in heat pump or A/C mode; not required to activate systems shut down, or operate cooling components when it is below sixty degrees (60 F) outside
facts.quote: (b) Operate the system using normal control devices and document temperature changes. Heat pump systems can be tested in either heat pump or A/C mode and should include emergency heat mode testing when readily accessible from thermostat controls. ... (2) The inspector is not required to: (a) Activate cooling systems that have been shut down. ... (e) Operate cooling system components if the exterior temperature is below sixty degrees Fahrenheit or when other circumstances are not conducive to safe operation or when doing so might damage the equipment.

facts.claim: WAC 308-408C-170 site: includes land grade and water drainage directly adjacent to the foundation, walks, driveways, patios, retaining walls contiguous with the structure; inspects condition of driveways, steps, walkways, patios and for proper grading and drainage slope; not required to evaluate hydrological or geological conditions
facts.quote: The inspection of the site includes the building perimeter, land grade, and water drainage directly adjacent to the foundation; trees and vegetation that adversely affect the structure; walks, grade steps, driveways, patios, and retaining walls contiguous with the structure. (1) The inspector will: ... (b) Inspect (i) The condition of the driveways, steps, walkways, patios, flatwork, and retaining walls contiguous with the structure. (ii) For proper grading and drainage slope. ... (2) The inspector is not required to: ... • Evaluate hydrological or geological conditions.

facts.claim: Fannie Mae B4-1.2-05 (12/10/2025): postponed improvements for NEW OR PROPOSED construction must be completed within 180 days of the note date; valid reasons include inclement weather; cost no more than 10% of as-completed value; completion escrow 120% of estimated cost
facts.quote: Requirements for New or Proposed Construction ... the postponed improvements must be completed within 180 days of the note date. Acceptable postponed items include items that: are part of the sales contract (third-party contracts are not permissible); are postponed for a valid reason, such as inclement weather or a shortage of building materials; ... The cost of completing improvements must not represent more than 10% of the “as completed” appraised value of the property. Lenders must establish a completion escrow for the postponed improvements, by withholding from the purchase proceeds funds equal to 120% of the estimated cost for completing the improvements.

facts.claim: Fannie Mae B4-1.2-05, existing construction: minor conditions/deferred maintenance not affecting safety, soundness or structural integrity may be escrowed at the lender's discretion; items that do affect them, e.g. active roof leaks, worn roof shingles, require a 'subject to' appraisal and the lender must verify completion before the loan is sold to Fannie Mae
facts.quote: If there are minor conditions or deferred maintenance items to be remedied or completed after closing, the lender may escrow for these items at its own discretion ... When an appraisal is required and there are incomplete items, physical deficiencies, or items affecting the safety, soundness, or structural integrity of the improvements, the appraisal must be "subject to" completion of the specific repairs or alterations. This may include but is not limited to foundation settlement, water seepage, active roof leaks, worn roof shingles, inadequate electrical service or plumbing fixtures, etc. ... In all cases, the lender must verify completion before the loan is sold to Fannie Mae.

facts.claim: Our report engine: roof_age full replacement $8,000 – $25,000+; hvac_age HVAC replacement $6,000 – $15,000; ENERGY STAR suggests considering replacement of an AC or heat pump over 10 years old, a furnace or boiler over 15
facts.quote: Full replacement $8,000 – $25,000+ ... HVAC replacement $6,000 – $15,000 ... ENERGY STAR suggests considering replacement once an air conditioner or heat pump is more than 10 years old, or a furnace or boiler more than 15.
